newsitem.title: USA: NYC wants bigger share of property tax relief plan.
newsitem.headline: NYC wants bigger share of property tax relief plan.

text.p: New York Gov George Pataki on Wednesday sweetened his property tax relief plan by making cooperative apartments eligible for the proposed savings, a move that would mainly help New York City.
Still, city officials said the plan, which is designed to lower property taxes earmarked for schools, still fell short.
"This is a small step in the right direction, but there is still substantial room for improvement before the city receives its fair share," New York City Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro said.

The administration of Mayor Rudy Guiliani argues that its public school students account for 37 to 38 percent of the state's student population, so that as a "matter of equity," it should receive the same percentage of tax relief under Pataki's $3.4 billion program.
The plan, which will be phased in over five years, entails $1.7 billion in property tax relief and $1.7 billion in additional state aid.

Mastro calculated that the governor's decision to make cooperative apartments eligible for the tax savings -- worth about $175 per cooperative or condominium apartment -- would raise the city's share of the total savings to 12 percent from nine percent.
The Pataki administration argues that the city for the first time will receive the correct proportion of school aid -- 37.5 percent -- under the preliminary budget.
To qualify for the new tax relief, school districts, which typically derive most or all of their funds from local property taxes, essentially would have to cap such levies.

New York City uses funds from a variety of sources to pay for its $9.0 billion school budget, and Mayor Rudolph Giuliani has said he is willing to negotiate setting limits on those other taxes with Pataki if that would give the city a bigger share of the tax relief.
"If that means talking about capping and relief on other taxes the city uses to pay for public education, the mayor said he's happy to talk about that," Mastro said.

The governor's preliminary budget, unveiled in late January, excluded the state's 260,000 cooperative apartments, a decision that fell particularly hard on New York City residents. The city has about 212,000 of the apartments.

"It is only fair that all New Yorkers who have worked and saved and invested in the American dream of ownership here in the Empire State are rewarded with lower property taxes -- whether they own homes, condos or co-ops," Pataki said in prepared remarks.

Pataki's decision to include cooperative apartments was announced as an amendment to his budget. On Thursday the governor will release his full list of amendments, said Michael McKeon, a spokesman for the governor. McKeon declined to comment on the other amendments.

New York City Council Speaker Peter Vallone has blasted the governor's property tax relief program for its failure to include co-ops, renters and owners of small buildings. And the governor's revised plan did not satisfy all his concerns.

"I am pleased that the governor is responding to my concerns about the inequities to New York City residents. We are now developing strategies that will include all types of households, not just those recognized by upstate," Vallone said in prepared comments.
